items.title: VisFlow: Interpretable Flow Matching for Visibility Reconstruction, Characterization, and Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.31892v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Methods for learning continuous representations, such as latent manifolds, are fundamental and ubiquitous in modern machine learning. Yet many geometric objects combine continuous shape information with discrete combinatorial structure. This combination presents a fundamental challenge for representation learning because small geometric perturbations can induce abrupt changes in the underlying discrete representation. As a result, the smoothness assumptions that make continuous representations effective no longer hold. Polygons provide a canonical example. Their vertex locations vary continuously, but infinitesimal changes in geometry can dramatically alter the associated visibility graph. Existing methods address the inverse mapping from visibility graphs to polygon geometry using vertex-, triangulation-, or signed-distance-function (SDF)-based representations. Vertex- and triangulation-based approaches construct polygons through explicit geometric operations. However, they are less effective at modeling the relationship between geometry and visibility. SDF-based approaches capture this relationship more naturally. Their intermediate states, however, do not correspond to explicit stages of polygon construction. We present VisFlow, a novel, interpretable flow formulation that combines continuous SDF representations with explicit polygon evolution. We evaluate VisFlow on Visibility Reconstruction and Visibility Characterization. Visibility Reconstruction generates one polygon consistent with a visibility graph (G), while Visibility Characterization characterizes all such polygons. VisFlow maintains 20% more visibility relations on Visibility Reconstruction and improves coverage by 30% on Visibility Characterization compared to state-of-the-art methods.

items.title: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training
items.content: arXiv:2610.32026v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary $z$-scores increasing from $+10.48$ to $+14.33$ on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from $-0.36$ to $+3.11$ on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative $L_2$ error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning.

items.title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.32216v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.

items.title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport
items.content: arXiv:2610.32660v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Continual Wi-Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi-Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per-class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed-form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new- and earlier-domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six-order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank-32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge-node storage budgets.
items.author: Chunchun Yang, Yang Cao, Zhitang Chen
items.summary: WiMoT enables continual Wi-Fi sensing without storing raw channel state information, addressing privacy and storage constraints in deployed sensing nodes. It stores per-class feature means and covariances and, when representations change, transports the stored statistics via an affine map on a frozen feature basis so they remain valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning plus a closed-form loss preserves class separability across domains.
items.reasoning: The moment-transport trick for keeping stored statistics valid under representation drift is elegant and the replay-free constraint is well motivated by privacy. The setting (Wi-Fi sensing) is specialized, but the continual-learning technique could interest the broader continual-learning community.

items.title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
items.content: arXiv:2610.31821v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state-of-the-art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment predicts BM25's behaviour, while embedding proximity predicts dense encoders. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known-item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open-weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal-match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what-the-query-remembers.

A single remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 recall points. This is a careful, culturally significant retrieval study with broad implications for query-composition effects.

items.title: Uni-Stream: A Unified Streaming Speech Language Model for Speech Synthesis and Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.32187v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Unified streaming speech language models aim to support speech recognition and synthesis within a single model, enabling real-time human-computer interaction. However, jointly supporting these two directions of speech-text conversion while preserving task-specific performance remains challenging. We propose Uni-Stream, a unified streaming speech language model built on compact pretrained speech models. Uni-Stream processes interleaved text and speech in a streaming format and achieves performance comparable to task-specific models through two-stage training. We also develop a data annotation pipeline for streaming training and will publicly release the generated transcriptions and word-level timestamps. We further examine Uni-Stream's representations across tasks and modalities and find that speech and text residence in distinct latent feature space even when trained in a unified model architecture, while representations within each modality become more task-dependent in later layers.

items.title: DIGOM: Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare
items.content: arXiv:2610.32451v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal healthcare data contain relational information that extends beyond individual patient observations. Effective clinical outcome prediction therefore requires not only integrating information from multiple modalities, but also modeling the relationships between them. Standard fusion approaches do not explicitly capture these interactions, while existing graph-based approaches typically model only a subset of them. We propose DIGOM (Disentangled Interaction Graphs for Outcome prediction in Multimodal healthcare), a graph-based framework that jointly models three complementary interaction types: Intra-patient cross-modal, Cross-patient same-modal, and Cross-patient cross-modal interactions. DIGOM learns a sparse multiplex graph with disentangled views, each encoding interactions between pairs of modalities across patients. Discrete adjacency matrices with patient-adaptive connectivity are sampled via a differentiable mechanism, enabling end-to-end learning and allowing the model to select informative relationships without imposing a fixed number of neighbors. A regularization objective maintains overall graph sparsity, while message passing integrates this relational context into patient representations for outcome prediction. We evaluate DIGOM on two multimodal healthcare datasets, MIMIC-IV and NIH-TB, across five clinical prediction tasks. DIGOM achieves the highest AUROC on all five tasks while using fewer connections than existing multi-interaction approaches. Ablation studies reveal that each interaction type's contribution varies across tasks, highlighting the need to adapt relational structures per task. DIGOM also demonstrates greater robustness to missing modalities, suggesting learned relationships provide complementary information when modalities are unavailable. Post-hoc analyses further reveal task- and outcome-specific connectivity patterns in the learned graphs.

items.title: EditJev: System One Routing for Image Editing Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.32635v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Instruction-based image editing models exhibit pronounced sample-specific performance variation: different models can produce substantially different results for the same source image and editing instruction, and the best-performing model often varies across requests. These models also differ substantially in inference latency, making fixed-model deployment inefficient. We therefore study image editing model routing, which dynamically selects an editor from a candidate pool given an input image and editing instruction. We introduce EditJev, a System One routing model that directly predicts sample-level preference scores over candidate image editing models in a single forward pass. A lightweight preference head on a vision-language backbone produces a fixed-dimensional score vector without autoregressive model-name generation or response parsing. To train EditJev, we construct pairwise preferences from offline candidate outputs and optimize a pairwise ranking objective to learn relative model suitability. At inference time, EditJev combines the predicted preference scores with model-level speed scores to balance editing quality and generation latency. Experiments on ImgEdit and GEdit-En show that EditJev improves aggregate quality over the strongest fixed editor, from 4.540 to 4.592 and from 8.194 to 8.255, respectively, while reducing estimated end-to-end latency by 60.8% and 31.7%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of direct, structured model routing for efficient image editing.

This exploits the fact that different editing models excel on different requests and differ in latency. Contributes to efficient, quality-aware model orchestration for generative editing.

items.title: AI Alignment for Digital Democracy: Fairer Voters Representation against LLM Biases
items.content: arXiv:2610.32780v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI representation is emerging in digital democracy, assisting in voter emulation and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) behave differently depending on the model, the prompt context, and the voter information they receive, representing some groups more accurately than others and potentially making the emulation unfair to certain groups. We investigate demographic biases in LLM-emulated electorates: how accurately LLMs represent individual votes, whether some voter groups are represented more accurately than others, and whether AI alignment can reduce these disparities without sacrificing overall accuracy. Using three U.S. presidential elections, we compare a closed-source and an open-source LLM across voters' demographic features and test AI alignment strategies toward fairer voter representation. Removing gender from the voter profile reduces the largest group error of the models by 22-42%, and removing education reduces it by 64%, whereas removing self-reported race increases the mean group error by over 40%, all without lowering accuracy. Common alignment strategies, such as repeated queries or fairness instructions, do not reduce these errors and can double them.
items.author: Yi Qi, Srijoni Majumdar, Evangelos Pournaras
items.summary: This work investigates demographic biases in LLM-emulated electorates for digital democracy, measuring how accurately LLMs reproduce individual votes across three U.S. presidential elections and whether some demographic groups are represented less fairly. The authors test whether alignment techniques can reduce inter-group disparities without sacrificing overall accuracy. It matters as AI-assisted voter representation raises real fairness-of-representation concerns.
items.reasoning: The empirical design over multiple real elections and both open and closed models is credible, and fairness of LLM voter emulation is a timely alignment-adjacent topic, but the application scope is specialized and the underlying finding that LLMs have demographic biases is fairly expected.

items.title: CuraLoc: Repository-Level Fault Localization via Planned Code Inspection
items.content: arXiv:2610.31809v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.
items.author: Sangeeta Warrier, Anush Sankaran, Ryen White
items.summary: CuraLoc improves repository-level fault localization by planning code inspection upfront rather than letting the LLM iteratively decide what to inspect, selecting candidate files, representing symbols compactly, and making a single joint planning decision over starting symbols, relationships to inspect, and edit hypotheses before deterministic retrieval. This reduces repeated model calls and token usage. It is relevant to scaling agentic software engineering economically.
items.reasoning: Planning-before-retrieval is a practical efficiency contribution to an active area (repository-level fault localization), with credible authors, but it refines an existing agentic paradigm rather than introducing a fundamentally new capability.

items.title: Aligning Large Language Models with Human Feedback: Mathematical Foundations and Algorithm Design
items.content: arXiv:2610.31862v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.
items.author: Siliang Zeng, Luca Viano, Chenliang Li, Jiaxiang Li, Volkan Cevher, Markus Wulfmeier, Stefano Ermon, Alfredo Garcia, Mingyi Hong
items.summary: A tutorial-style survey covering the mathematical foundations of LLM alignment, including SFT, RLHF, and DPO, and connecting preference learning to inverse reinforcement learning and discrete choice models. Authored by a strong team including Stefano Ermon and Markus Wulfmeier, it aims to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers entering the alignment field.
items.reasoning: High author credibility and a useful unifying treatment connecting RLHF theory to IRL, but as a tutorial it offers limited original research novelty. Valuable as an educational and reference resource.

items.title: Curvature-Aware Clipping: Mitigating Bias in DPSGD via Approximate Second-Order Information
items.content: arXiv:2610.32175v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) has become the de facto standard for training deep neural networks with rigorous privacy guarantees. However, the utility of DPSGD is constrained by gradient clipping bias and DP noise. While existing work has tried to address these issues, the geometric misalignment caused by clipping bias remains a critical challenge. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, Curvature-Aware Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (CA-DPSGD), which leverages approximate second-order information to construct an optimal, curvature-aware clipping space. CA-DPSGD integrates a rectified estimator for the curvature matrix and is coupled with an anisotropic noise mechanism to ensure privacy guarantees. Extensive empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art clipping methods.
items.author: Xincheng Xu, Thilina Ranbaduge, Thierry Rakotoarivelo, David Smith
items.summary: CA-DPSGD mitigates the gradient-clipping bias in differentially private training by using approximate second-order curvature information to construct an optimal clipping space, with a rectified curvature estimator and anisotropic noise for privacy. This addresses geometric misalignment that existing clipping approaches leave unresolved.
items.reasoning: Differentially private training utility is an important and persistent problem, and the curvature-aware clipping angle is a reasonable advance. Impact tempered by the specialized privacy-training audience and added computational cost of second-order estimates.

items.title: Recommender regret for improving regularised RL estimation with bandits and MCTS
items.content: arXiv:2610.32910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms rely on estimators, like Monte Carlo tree search or one-step look-ahead, to provide policy, value, or Q-value estimates in training and inference. However, existing bandit-based estimation frameworks evaluate sampling efficiency, not the quality of estimates. We address this by formalising estimate generation as a recommendation process, treating bandit-based sampling as an improvement operator. To evaluate the quality of a recommendation (estimate), we define regulariser-aware recommender regrets, analysing their lower bounds, and proving that simple algorithms like uniform sampling can achieve these bounds. Finally, we unify bandit- and search-based target improvement under recommender MCTS. Across synthetic trees, arcade games, and scientific discovery tasks, recommenders often yield faster target convergence and superior downstream performance. Our experiments characterise for the first time the potential of regularised MCTS in scientific applications.
items.author: Danilo Vucetic, Alexandre Larouche, Mohammad Pedramfar, Audrey Durand, Gauthier Gidel
items.summary: The paper formalizes estimate generation in regularized RL (via bandit sampling, MCTS, or look-ahead) as a recommendation process and introduces regulariser-aware recommender regrets to measure estimate quality rather than just sampling efficiency. It analyzes lower bounds, shows simple algorithms like uniform sampling achieve them, and unifies bandit- and search-based target improvement under a common framework.
items.reasoning: A useful conceptual unification of bandit and search estimation in RL with new regret notions, but it is more of a reframing than an algorithmic breakthrough and its practical consequences remain to be demonstrated.

items.title: Neural Disjunctive Normal Forms for Learning Exact Rank Filters
items.content: arXiv:2610.32203v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Gradient-based learning of morphological operators is hindered by locally sparse derivatives with respect to the structuring elements. We develop a method for learning rank filters that retains exact operator evaluation while distributing the derivatives across the window. Using threshold decomposition, we construct a neural disjunctive normal form representation and establish a sufficient condition for exactness with integer-valued images and structuring elements. We then derive a smooth surrogate from the unique root of a smooth threshold equation. Implicit differentiation gives closed-form derivatives with normalised local weights, whose distribution is controlled by a smoothing parameter. These derivatives are used in a straight-through procedure: the forward pass evaluates the exact rank filter, while the backward pass uses the surrogate. For fixed ranks, the procedure learns real-valued structuring elements of any rank filter, including the median, and extends to compositions, infima, and suprema of rank filters. Experiments on image denoising using MNIST and Fashion-MNIST and retinal vessel segmentation show that, starting from a generic random initialisation, the proposed approach consistently improves performance over training with exact subgradients in every setting. In image denoising, our best network also outperforms smooth morphological networks in all settings. On vessel segmentation, the learned erosions recover structuring elements that fit the vessels, as theoretically expected, whereas most of those trained with exact subgradients remain close to their initialisation.
items.author: Diego Marcondes, Wonder A. L. Alves, Ronaldo F. Hashimoto
items.summary: The paper develops a method for gradient-based learning of morphological rank filters by constructing a neural disjunctive normal form via threshold decomposition, retaining exact operator evaluation while distributing derivatives across the window. A smooth surrogate with closed-form derivatives from implicit differentiation enables straight-through-style training. This addresses the locally sparse derivative problem that has hindered learning of morphological operators.
items.reasoning: Technically elegant solution to a genuine differentiability problem in morphological learning, with exactness guarantees for integer-valued images. The niche domain limits broad impact, but the technique could extend to other non-differentiable operator learning problems.

items.title: PathJev: Decision-Native Vision-Language Modelling for Histopathology
items.content: arXiv:2610.32478v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language models used for decisions in histopathology rarely return calibrated probabilities over the candidates a user cares about. Decision-native models write a question and a candidate set chosen at run time into the input and return a normalised distribution from a small decision head in one forward pass. We build PathJev-P, a decision-native model for histopathology: MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections whose expert labels are turned into typed questions with organ-specific candidate sets and a "none of these" option. In a comparison over 3 seeds with an analysis plan fixed before testing, on test sets without documented overlap with the training data of the backbone, PathJev-P is more accurate than a generative model trained with the same backbone, data and selection rule, the zero-shot pathology model CONCH and a general medical decision model (balanced accuracy 0.541 against 0.492, 0.345 and 0.213); its advantage over the generative model comes from two organs absent from training. The calibration advantage depends on how the generative model's probabilities are read out. With the summed candidate log-likelihood used in previous work, PathJev-P has the lower calibration error (ECE 0.204 against 0.279); with a length-normalised read-out of the same generative model, examined post hoc, the two have similar mean calibration error (0.201) and the generative model is better calibrated on the unseen organs, where PathJev-P remains over-confident. A supervised linear probe on a pathology foundation model is better calibrated in every setting. In a qualitative whole-slide demonstration, PathJev-P labels unsupervised tissue clusters with abstention and separates carcinoma from other tissue while running the model on a fraction of the tiles.
items.author: Cristian Tommasino, Antonio M. Rinaldi
items.summary: PathJev-P builds a decision-native histopathology model on MedGemma-1.5-4B with LoRA adapters and a decision head that returns calibrated distributions over run-time candidate sets, trained on 40,000 patch states from three public collections. Evaluation follows a pre-registered analysis plan across seeds on test sets without documented training overlap.
items.reasoning: The decision-native formulation with typed questions and none-of-these options, plus rigorous pre-specified evaluation methodology, is a thoughtful contribution to trustworthy clinical VLMs. Impact is bounded by the 4B-scale base model and benchmark setting, but the methodology is strong.

items.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
items.content: arXiv:2610.32854v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.
items.author: Kamillo Ferry, Anthea Monod, Keisuke Yano
items.summary: The paper studies LoRA through the lens of singular learning theory, using the real log canonical threshold to characterize learning complexity that parameter dimension alone cannot capture due to the low-rank factorization's non-identifiability. Under a local linearization, a forward-backward covariance built from activations and backpropagated sensitivities determines which directions of the pretrained network are learnable.
items.reasoning: Applying RLCT-based singular learning theory to LoRA is a novel and rigorous theoretical treatment of an ubiquitous fine-tuning method, yielding potentially actionable insights about which directions are learnable; the local linearization assumption limits direct practical reach.

items.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
items.content: arXiv:2610.32955v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. On 739 real Italian/English emails labelled by the owner (231 unbiased, 500 adversarially sampled), we compare nine systems under thread-grouped cross-validation: the production keyword rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble), a hosted decision model (Nimble v4-max), and hosted generative LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma 4 26B/31B). Four results. The production rules score 28% on message type against a 58% majority class: the field shown most prominently carried no information. With ~200 labels, logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90), though it never predicts the two rarest classes and is statistically tied with Gemma 4 on type; few-shot prompting does not close the gap. The sender's relationship (client, supplier, service) is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy where the contact has been seen, and is not inferable from a single message by any model: it belongs in the contact graph, not the prompt. Finally, accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the most accurate system most often ignores emails needing action (18% vs 4% for the best LLM); a cost-chosen threshold on its noise probability halves that rate and makes it the cheapest system.

items.title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.32002v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
items.author: Siyang He, Qiqi Wang, Fan Liu, Yuncheng Huang, Pengfei Xu, Xi Chen, Ziwei He, Xipeng Qiu
items.summary: DraMaze is a multi-agent pipeline for long-form microdrama script generation that explores diverse causal paths via trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation, and constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize and retrieve historical memories relevant to future plots. It addresses plot convergence and trope reuse observed as LLM generation progresses. The work targets the growing microdrama production market.
items.reasoning: A creative application with genuinely interesting architectural ideas (future-aware memory, backward dependency trees, evolutionary search over narrative paths) from a strong group including Xipeng Qiu. However, it is application-specific and evaluation of creative generation quality is inherently subjective.

items.title: Disentangling Question, Response, and Verifier Languages in Multilingual P(True) Self-Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.32144v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a language model is asked whether its own answer is correct, three languages are involved: that of the question, that requested for the answer, and that of the verifier instruction asking for the judgment. Multilingual confidence evaluations seldom separate the three. We vary them independently in a six-language factorial design with ten open-weight models (3B-14B) on LSQA, MMMLU and TriviaQA, holding each answer fixed across verifier languages and measuring confidence with a first-token P(True) probe. The three languages move different parts of the evaluation: which of them governs accuracy depends on the benchmark, matching the response language to the question or verifier language sharpens discrimination but not calibration, and the verifier language alone shifts calibration error by up to 0.04 without changing accuracy. The scorer matters as well: an unvalidated judge would have shrunk the MMMLU English-Hindi accuracy gap from 0.198 to 0.038. Multilingual confidence results, model rankings included, are therefore comparable only when all three languages are reported and the scorer is validated.
items.author: Jewon Yeom, Jaewon Sok, Seonghyeon Park, Jeongjae Park, Hwiyeong Lee, Taesup Kim
items.summary: The paper presents a six-language factorial study of multilingual self-evaluation, independently varying the language of the question, the requested response, and the verifier instruction across ten open-weight models (3B-14B). It finds the three languages affect accuracy and discrimination differently, and that matching response language to question or verifier language sharpens discrimination without improving calibration.
items.reasoning: A careful, well-designed factorial analysis of an overlooked confound in multilingual confidence estimation, with practical implications for deploying self-evaluation in multilingual settings. The scope (P(True) probing on open-weight models up to 14B) limits generality to larger or proprietary models, but the disentangling methodology is a solid contribution.

items.title: Residual Expert Routing for Text-Only Domain Adaptation of Factorized Transducer ASR
items.content: arXiv:2610.32637v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fine-tuning the non-blank predictor of a factorized transducer on target-domain text improves recognition on that domain but degrades performance on the source domain. A single interpolation weight between base and adapted predictors cannot resolve this: the adapted predictor helps at some prefixes and hurts at others, often within one utterance. We propose conservative residual routing: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, and a 16k-parameter gate decides at each prefix how much of it to admit. Closing the gate reproduces the base exactly. On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retains essentially all of the text-only gain on two held-out domains (19.89 to 16.74, 20.91 to 16.21 WER) while leaving source-domain WER unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone costs 1.08 WER. Routing needs no per-domain tuning on target-domain audio. Analysis reveals the gate does not behave as a simple domain-level switch: it modulates intervention through the disagreement between the two predictors, suppressing it in-domain and amplifying it out-of-domain.
items.author: Shashi Kumar, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
items.summary: The paper proposes conservative residual routing for domain-adapting factorized transducer ASR: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, with a 16k-parameter gate deciding per prefix how much to admit. This retains nearly all text-only adaptation gains on held-out domains while preserving source-domain performance, solving a problem that static interpolation weights cannot.
items.reasoning: An elegant, lightweight solution to a well-defined problem (catastrophic degradation under domain adaptation), with clear WER evidence and minimal parameter overhead. The contribution is incremental within the ASR engineering literature but is well-executed and immediately practical.

items.title: SPOOK: Sparse Pixel Optimization for Off-Manifold Knowledge in Vision Encoders
items.content: arXiv:2610.32835v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern vision encoders are widely used as semantic representations, but the relationship between embedding similarity and human-visible semantics can become unclear far from the natural-image manifold. We probe this regime in a black-box setting by applying sparse pixel edits to blank canvases with a simple pixel-level hill-climbing procedure. Across ImageNet and Flickr30k, we evaluate whether these edited blank canvases can retrieve chosen targets in multimodal contrastive encoders and self-supervised visual encoders. On OpenCLIP, inputs optimized toward class prompts achieve strong top-1 and top-5 targeted retrieval performance; on DINOv3, inputs optimized toward class prototypes achieve high target alignment and near-top prototype ranks. These results show that sparse edits on otherwise blank, visually non-semantic inputs can enter target semantic basins in both language-aligned and self-supervised visual representation spaces. Our findings identify a shared off-manifold failure mode of modern vision encoders and suggest sparse blank-canvas optimization as a simple probe of representation geometry.
items.author: Ankit Gupta, Akshat Pandya, Christoph Adami, Emily Dolson
items.summary: SPOOK probes vision encoders far from the natural-image manifold using black-box sparse pixel edits on blank canvases optimized by hill-climbing. This exposes a security-relevant weakness in widely used vision encoders.
items.reasoning: A clean adversarial analysis revealing that embedding similarity breaks down off the natural-image manifold, with implications for retrieval security. The finding is notable but incremental relative to the large adversarial examples literature, and the truncated abstract limits assessment of breadth.

items.title: LOCI: Localized Continuous Control for Multi-Subject Image Editing
items.content: arXiv:2610.31950v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent instruction-following image editors such as Flux.1-Kontext enable text-driven editing but lack fine-grained control over where and how much an edit is applied. Existing approaches provide either continuous but global control or spatially localized editing at a fixed strength. To our knowledge, none jointly supports explicit spatial localization, continuous per-region strength, and independent simultaneous control of multiple subjects. We present LOCI (LOcalized Continuous control for multi- subject Image editing). Given a multi-subject image with per-subject regions and instructions, LOCI edits each subject at an independently chosen, continuously adjustable strength, for instance gradually aging one person while adding a beard to another with minimal cross-region leakage. LOCI pairs subject-level attention binding for spatial isolation with a Regional LoRA layer that replaces the LoRA's scalar coefficient with a per-token scaling vector aligned to the spatial layout. A single adapter is trained at one suppression point, and continuous edit strengths follow by rescaling its regional residual at inference. Experiments on multi-subject scenes demonstrate that LOCI achieves strong edit fidelity with significantly reduced cross-region interference compared to baselines, while maintaining continuous control over edit strength
items.author: Sai Vidyaranya Nuthalapati, Shlok Kumar Mishra

For example, it can gradually age one person while adding a beard to another at independently chosen strengths. This addresses a real controllability gap in current text-driven image editing.
items.reasoning: A useful controllability contribution building on Flux.1-Kontext, an established editor, with a clear unification of previously separate capabilities. Impact is bounded by reliance on a specific base editor and the fast-moving image editing field, but the control interface is broadly applicable.

items.title: Towards Effective and Transferable Physical Camouflage against Multi-View BEV-based 3D Perception in Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2610.32230v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern autonomous driving systems widely adopt multi-view Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) based 3D perception models due to their superior performance. Despite their success, the robustness of these models against adversarial camouflage attacks remains largely unexplored. Existing camouflage attacks primarily target single-view 2D detectors, limiting their effectiveness in multi-view 3D perception settings. To address this gap, we propose BEVCA, a novel adversarial camouflage generation framework tailored for multi-view BEV-based 3D perception. Our framework integrates a BEV-feature-based adversarial loss with a multi-view neural rendering module, enabling effective and transferable camouflage attacks across different models and tasks. Extensive experiments in both digital and physical settings demonstrate that BEVCA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and exhibits strong robustness under real-world conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/WAVE-AT-IDEA/BEVCA.
items.author: Linye Lyu, Jiawei Zhou, Daojing He, Yu Li
items.summary: Presents BEVCA, an adversarial physical camouflage framework targeting multi-view BEV-based 3D perception in autonomous driving, combining BEV-feature adversarial losses with multi-view neural rendering for transferable attacks across models and tasks. It exposes previously unexplored robustness gaps in BEV perception systems.
items.reasoning: Safety-relevant adversarial research on BEV perception is important for autonomous driving robustness, and extending physical attacks from 2D single-view to multi-view 3D settings is a genuine gap. Value is primarily defensive (revealing vulnerabilities), with some dual-use concern typical of adversarial ML work.

items.title: Fast and Useful: Adapting Distilled Generators for Visual Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.32512v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distilled text-to-image models generate images quickly, but classifiers trained on those images can perform substantially worse than classifiers trained on images from their slower base models. We adapt released distilled generators to produce better training data while retaining fast generation. We fit a low-rank update to the student's first prediction so that it reaches an intermediate state produced by its unguided base, then disable the update and let the unchanged student finish generation. The base supplies training targets and is absent at inference. Guided targets and shorter jumps give classifiers lower accuracy in our ablations, showing why the state used for supervision matters. Across three generator families, the adapted images train better classifiers than images from the released students. With class-name templates at full ImageNet-1k scale, ResNet-50 top-1 rises from 8.4% to 34.2% for FLUX.2-klein and from 12.7% to 32.1% for SD-Turbo, using two and three denoiser evaluations per image, respectively. Fixed adapters also improve results on additional classes, fine-grained datasets, and other learner architectures and training recipes. Template-based adaptation remains useful against richer-prompt alternatives, while the benefit of combining adaptation with LLM generation prompts depends on the generator. Adapting a single generation step makes fast generators substantially more useful for training visual models.
items.author: Patryk Bartkowiak, Dominik Michels, S\"oren Pirk, Wojciech Pa{\l}ubicki
items.summary: This paper identifies that classifiers trained on images from distilled fast text-to-image generators underperform those trained on base-model outputs, and adapts released distilled generators by fitting a low-rank update toward an intermediate base-model state before letting the student finish generation. Ablations show why the supervision state matters, and adapted images improve classifier training across three generator families while staying fast.
items.reasoning: Addresses a timely and practical problem with synthetic data quality from distilled generators, and the finding about which generation state to use for supervision is an interesting mechanistic insight. The technique is clever but narrowly scoped to synthetic-data training pipelines.

items.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
items.content: arXiv:2610.32554v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
items.author: I-tak Ieong, Hao Tang
items.summary: HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory in a hierarchical world model for zero-shot object navigation, using coarse visual-semantic heading scoring and fine symbolic graph matching, with phase-dependent fusion. It reports 62.6 percent SR and 31.5 SPL on HM3D and 46.8 percent SR on MP3D, improving over WMNav. This advances evidence-retaining zero-shot embodied navigation.
items.reasoning: Solid benchmark gains on standard navigation datasets with a reasonable combination of LLM priors, memory, and graph matching; the architecture is a composition of existing ideas and gains are moderate rather than transformative.

items.title: Robotic Optical Coherence Tomography-Guided Geometric Modeling of Soft Tissue: 3D Representations for Data-Driven Closed-Loop Shape Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.32961v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In medical robotics, data-driven soft-tissue shape control requires deforming tissue toward desired morphologies through sequential physical interactions. This challenge is particularly important in microscale manipulation, where localized deformation is difficult to observe, represent, and control, while physics-based models can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to realistic environments. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, but target-conditioned control requires effective representations of both observed and desired tissue states. In this work, we introduce an OCT-guided data-driven framework for tissue shape control, learned from user-guided demonstrations and executed with closed-loop OCT feedback. We study full-volume, tissue-masked sparse-volume, and voxelized point-cloud representations, with or without residual conditioning, using deterministic (Explicit) and generative diffusion (Diffusion) policies. Across 12 configurations and 576 phantom rollouts on 3-DoF depth and 6-DoF directional tasks, OCT-derived 3D representations support both Explicit and Diffusion policies, with performance depending on representation and residual conditioning. Residual conditioning reduces directional Shape RMSE from 0.748 to 0.555 mm for full-volume Diffusion, while voxelized point-cloud Explicit with residuals achieves 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control, with comparable accuracy at intermediate unseen targets and consistent performance across deployments. We further evaluate the framework in 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts, extending to biological tissue with final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations. These results establish volumetric OCT as current and goal representations for learned closed-loop tissue shape control across deterministic and generative action models.
items.author: Chaoyu Zhang, Guangshen Ma, Mark Draelos
items.summary: This paper introduces an OCT-guided data-driven framework for closed-loop soft-tissue shape control in medical robotics, learned from user-guided demonstrations. Optical coherence tomography provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, and the work builds 3D representations of observed and desired tissue states to support target-conditioned control at microscales where physics-based models are expensive. The approach aims to enable data-driven tissue manipulation where localized deformation is hard to observe and model.
items.reasoning: Combines a distinctive sensing modality (robotic OCT) with learned representations for a genuinely hard problem in microscale medical manipulation. Novelty is good and the medical robotics application is impactful, but the framework is early-stage and validated in limited settings, so broad significance is not yet established.

items.title: From Visual Affinity to Learning Credit in Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.32324v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves multimodal reasoning, but uniformly assigning a single response-level advantage to all tokens overlooks the distinct roles of visual observations and subsequent reasoning. Visual affinity alone is insufficient: predictive states may align with both image and prompt-context representations, and upweighting valid visual observations can amplify their negative-advantage updates when later reasoning fails. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{Outcome-Conditioned Visual Credit (OVC)}, a plug-in framework that separates visual-association measurement from token-level credit assignment and is adaptable to policy-optimization methods with uniform response-level advantage allocation. Relative Visual Encoding constructs a context-relative visual coordinate by contrasting each predictive state's affinity to image and prompt-context representations. Outcome-conditioned Evidence Calibration combines this coordinate with uncertainty-scaled predictive features and calibrates their contributions to outcome-discriminative evidence through mean contrasts between positive- and negative-advantage responses, scaled by regularized within-side variation. Visual association thus informs credit through observed outcome differences rather than directly determining update priority. Normalized Credit Allocation conditions the calibrated evidence on the response's advantage sign to produce positive token weights with unit global mean. These detached weights preserve advantage signs while modulating individual token-gradient contributions. OVC reuses existing rollouts without auxiliary reward models, process annotations, or inference-time modules. Instantiated through GSPO-token, OVC retains sequence-level clipping and consistently improves six-benchmark mean accuracy over GSPO across three models, with gains of 1.86-2.39 percentage points.

items.title: SemGeo-Gen: Unsupervised Generation of Approximate Cross-Instance Semantic-Geometric Correspondences
items.content: arXiv:2610.32663v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce SemGeo-Gen, an unsupervised method for generating approximate cross-instance semantic-geometric supervision from weakly aligned 3D object collections. Our goal is not to recover exact point-level correspondences, which are often ambiguous across different instances and would require expensive, impractical manual supervision at scale. Instead, we automatically produce approximate correspondences that are semantically meaningful, geometrically consistent, and diverse enough to train modern correspondence models. Given only coarse category-level rotation alignment, SemGeo-Gen lifts multi-view DINOv2 features to 3D, aligns object instances using continuous piecewise-affine registration, and prunes candidate matches using semantic consistency. The resulting 3D correspondences can be projected into rendered views, yielding scalable 3D-3D, 3D-2D, and 2D-2D supervision without manual annotation. We validate the generated correspondences against sparse human annotations from KeypointNet, obtaining 93% PCK@0.10 and 97% PCK@0.15. More importantly, we show that using the generated correspondences for synthetic pretraining improves recent state-of-the-art semantic correspondence models on SPair-71k after fine-tuning on real data, with gains of up to 5 PCK@0.10 points. Together, these results indicate that approximate semantic-geometric supervision generated from 3D assets can improve real-image correspondence learning and serve as a scalable alternative to costly manual annotation. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/SemGeo-Gen/.

items.title: Reading Between the Layers: Cross-Modal Alignment and Representational Hierarchy in Vision Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.32463v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While large vision-language models excel at optical character recognition, it remains unclear how their underlying vision encoders process text and its meaning, and whether they support anything resembling reading comprehension. We systematically study transformer-based vision encoders, using cross-modal alignment between rendered text and visual concepts together with probing and retrieval-based analyses as a controlled window into these broader capabilities. Our layer-wise analyses span orthographic, grammatical, and semantic organization, and reveal that strong cross-modal mapping emerges only in the deepest layers, after unimodal object and text recognition have already developed, coinciding with a progression from surface-level to semantic representations. Although this hierarchy is strongest in contrastively trained models, larger self-supervised models and text-rich training data partially support similar behaviors without explicit language supervision. Together, our results suggest that increasing model and training-data scale, as well as text-rich training data, can partially compensate for the absence of language supervision.

items.title: STEP: Surgical Point Tracking from Sparse Endpoints and Pseudo-trajectories
items.content: arXiv:2610.31951v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Surgical point tracking requires persistent correspondence through tissue deformation and occlusion, yet dense trajectory annotations are costly to obtain. We present STEP, a two-stage framework that learns from surgical video and sparse physical endpoints. First, a frozen offline teacher generates candidate trajectories, and temporal reversibility and stereo consistency select dense supervision for a causal student. Second, a robust physical endpoint loss anchors terminal correspondence, while a round-trip loss constrains temporal consistency. A gradient-free prefix exposes training to accumulated drift, while a final differentiable window bounds activation memory. The trained tracker processes a single RGB stream with fixed weights. In STIR-to-VL-SurgPT transfer, temporal-stereo union selection reduces endpoint error by 7.0% relative to unfiltered trajectories. On a post-hoc diagnostic of 29 VL-SurgPT clips excluded from the endpoint-training manifest, STEP reduces endpoint error from 31.52 to 16.80 pixels relative to dense-label fine-tuning. These results support combining curated trajectories with physical observations to train surgical point trackers.

items.title: Sounding Surgical Instrument Localisation through Audio-Visual Correspondence
items.content: arXiv:2610.32816v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Surgical scene understanding is a prerequisite for context-aware and intelligent systems in the operating room. Current methods rely mostly on visual data, while acoustic sensing has shown potential to provide complementary information on surgical activity. First approaches for the localisation of surgical activity relied on microphone arrays and acoustic beamforming. This work investigates whether the active instrument can be localized from a single microphone and a camera by learning the correspondence between the appearance and the sound of surgical instruments, without annotating its position. We adapt weakly supervised audio-visual localisation, which learns from the co-occurrence of image and sound, to the surgical setting. We record simulated surgical actions, sawing, drilling, and chiseling, and train the model on these recordings without any spatial annotation to produce a heatmap over the sounding tool. We extend the training objective by two terms: a silence term, which suppresses the output for silence and background noise, and a composite term, which trains the model to select the sounding one of two visible instruments. The model localizes the active instrument on an independent corpus recorded with a different camera and microphone, in which instrument positions were obtained by optical tracking. It separates tool activity from silence and background noise and can attribute sound correctly when two tools are present. Audio-visual correspondence learned from in-domain recordings connects the sound of a surgical action to the instrument that produces it, using a single microphone and a camera. This proof of concept introduces a novel paradigm that enables the detection and localisation of surgical activity without manual annotations.

items.title: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.32087v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

items.title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports
items.content: arXiv:2610.32258v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in clinical documentation, generating the rigorous, evidence-based reasoning required for unprecedented, atypical, and rare disease case reports remains a significant challenge. We present MedCaseAgent, an end-to-end agentic reasoning paradigm that bridges this gap by synthesizing publication-quality reports from unstructured clinical notes. MedCaseAgent leverages a hierarchical structure, integrating patient-level data mining with iterative, tool-integrated reasoning. By dynamically querying medical literature and knowledge bases, the agent maintains high clinical fidelity and assesses case novelty. The framework is inherently modular, supporting various backbone LLMs in a plug-and-play fashion. To facilitate this research, we release MedCase-150K, a large-scale multimodal clinical case-report corpus, and MedCase-Bench, a robust temporally held-out evaluation suite. We also introduce an open-source model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and optimized specifically for this task. Under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents. Blinded expert reviews and ablations further support the system's clinical relevance and evidence grounding.

items.title: Adaptive Control of Scientific Instruments with Nonstationary Responses through Multimodal Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.32370v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.

items.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
items.content: arXiv:2610.32477v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.

It aims to give long-horizon agents human-like causal understanding of their environment.

items.title: Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication
items.content: arXiv:2610.32738v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities. We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazard-map production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts. We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners. The generated maps improved participants' spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps. We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication.
items.author: Sidi Wu, Lifeng Lin, Yizi Chen, Anna Yokokubo, Lorenz Hurni

Informed by a formative study with map experts and validated via user studies with practitioners, generated maps improved spatial understanding and evacuation planning. items.title: Rethinking Structured Generation: Can Graph-Based Reasoning Resolve Ambiguity?
items.content: arXiv:2610.31681v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Structured generation is typically formulated as a deterministic mapping from input to a single structured output. This assumption is fundamentally misaligned with natural language, which often admits multiple structurally distinct yet semantically valid interpretations. As a result, existing methods rely on single-reference supervision that collapses ambiguity into one prediction, leading to unstable and inconsistent outputs under underspecified inputs. We reformulate structured generation as an \textit{ambiguity-aware inference problem}, where the objective is to reason over a set of plausible structured outputs rather than predict a single solution. We show that standard training inherently suppresses valid alternatives, and instead adopt a multi-valid learning framework that preserves ambiguity during optimization. To operationalize this formulation, we construct a candidate space of structured outputs, represent each candidate as a graph capturing entities and their relationships, and perform selection via graph-based reasoning over semantic alignment and relational consistency. This enables principled comparison across competing interpretations beyond token-level likelihoods. Experiments on structured generation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, stability, and robustness under varying levels of ambiguity. These results highlight the importance of modeling ambiguity explicitly and suggest a shift from single-output prediction to set-level reasoning in structured generation.

items.title: What Open-Source Projects Tell Their Coding Agents: A Census of AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
items.content: arXiv:2610.31715v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Coding agents can be guided with instruction files in a repository. We examine this emerging practice through a census of popular, active GitHub repositories in thirteen languages, treating each repository's root AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md as one instruction set. Agent instructions appear in of repositories and of the most-starred; where both files exist, CLAUDE.md usually points to AGENTS.md. We analyse statements using model-assisted annotation and human review. The annotations reveal a practical mix of project knowledge and rules about code, building and workflow. Collaboration rules name concrete requirements, from test plans to commit formats, yet of directives give no reason. Projects disagree on AI attribution: commit-message rules more often prohibit it than require it, while pull-request rules more often require disclosure. A third of instruction sets have a generator-associated signature, a tool-inserted block, shared text or an AI-marked creation commit; four in five are edited after creation. Prespecified tests associate repository popularity with rules on pull requests and AI contributions. Exploratory analyses link activity to process-oriented content and show that LLM and agent projects are over-represented among adopters. The models agree much more closely with each other than with the human reviewer's topic assignments, a caution for automated annotation. We release the annotations, taxonomies and pointers to the analysed file versions.

It documents an emerging de facto practice for steering coding agents in the wild.

items.title: MI-MIDI 2: From Observation to Control with Sparse Autoencoders in Text-to-MIDI Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.32007v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can expose features of a generative model without predefined labels, but in language models the evidence used to interpret these features has proven an unreliable guide to which of them steer the output. Whether interpretations of SAE features predict control in music generators has not, to our knowledge, been tested. We develop an end-to-end protocol for discovering and evaluating SAE features in text-to-MIDI generation and apply it to text2midi and MIDI-LLM. The protocol characterizes features through correlations with musical metrics, shared instrument programs, and automated descriptions, each with its own control: note-density adjustment, matched inactive excerpts, and permutation calibration. It then tests candidates by intervention, measured directly in the generated MIDI against unmodified generation and a matched random direction, ranks them in screens, and confirms selected features on new prompts. Evidence that survives these controls points to features that steer the output. Descriptions exceed permutation controls for instrumentation, and a feature whose description names a synth-lead program introduces that program in a prespecified confirmation and in a replication on disjoint prompts and reappears in independently trained dictionaries. Features selected by density-adjusted correlations show a small positive shift of their target metric as a family, whereas features selected by raw correlations show none. An atlas provides MIDI, piano-roll, and audio examples for every feature of the targeted screen.

items.title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.32212v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.
items.author: Jiawei Dong, Zilong Bai, Pengtian zhu, Peng Zhou
items.summary: SOPO is a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework for span-level hallucination detection that addresses localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and length inflation that challenge standard RLVR. Its key innovation is a Socratic feedback mechanism in which a teacher model guides reasoning trajectories during rollouts. This is relevant to improving the factuality of LLM outputs at a fine-grained level.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated extension of verifiable-reward RL to an important safety-relevant NLP task, with a novel teacher-guided feedback mechanism. Task-specific scope and early-stage results temper the score.
